etymology: From Latin profanus, before or outside the temple: the quality of treating what God has set apart as common. Webster 1828 keeps the word for irreverence of sacred things, especially speech that takes the name of God in vain.
biblical_def: Profaneness is irreverence toward what the LORD has called holy. He forbids swearing by His name falsely and profaning the name of God (Lev 19:12). Priests profane Him when they put no difference between the holy and the profane and hide their eyes from His sabbaths (Eze 22:26). The law is made for the unholy and profane, not as a ladder for the righteous but as a curb on men who treat God as common (1 Tim 1:9). The sin is not coarse manners alone. It is the heart that will not fear the Name.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PROFA'NENESS as irreverence of sacred things; particularly, the use of language which implies irreverence towards God; the taking of God's name in vain.
webster_full: PROFA'NENESS, noun — Irreverence of sacred things; particularly, the use of language which implies irreverence towards God; the taking of God's name in vain.
Profaneness in men is vulgar and odious; in females, is shocking and detestable.
scriptures: Leviticus 19:12
And ye shall not swear by my name falsely, neither shalt thou profane the name of thy God: I am the LORD.
Ezekiel 22:26

Her priests have violated my law, and have profaned mine holy things: they have put no difference between the holy and profane, neither have they shewed difference between the unclean and the clean, and have hid their eyes from my sabbaths, and I am profaned among them.
corruption_summary: The age treats profaneness as flavor in speech, comedy, or intensity, and no longer as irreverence of sacred things.
corruption_paragraphs: Casual oaths, film dialogue, and locker-room wit take the name of God as punctuation. That is the old sin under a new excuse. Webster still named it vulgar and odious. Scripture names it profaning the Name of the LORD.

A second drift calls reverence optional style and profaneness authenticity. The dictionary will not baptize that. Holy and profane are not taste categories. God Himself draws the line, and priests fall when they erase it.
roots_summary: The English noun names a quality Scripture describes by the verb to profane and by the adjective profane. No Strong's number is invented for the later abstract noun.
roots_lines: English profaneness — irreverence of sacred things, especially vain use of the name of God.
KJV profane marks what is common over against what the LORD has hallowed (Eze 22:26; 1 Tim 1:9).
No invented Strong's tag for the abstract English noun.
usage: Profaneness is irreverence of holy things, not a colorful personality.
Do not swear by the name of the LORD falsely, and do not treat His Name as common speech.
Keep the difference between the holy and the profane.

etymology: From Latin in and poenitens, from poeniteo, to repent, and poena, pain: the want of repentance. Webster 1828 pairs the word with obduracy and hardness of heart.
biblical_def: Impenitence is the refusal to sorrow for sin and turn. Paul names the impenitent heart that, after hardness, treasures up wrath against the day of wrath (Rom 2:5). The man often reproved who hardens his neck shall be destroyed suddenly, and that without remedy (Prov 29:1). Christ gave Jezebel space to repent, and she repented not (Rev 2:21). Final impenitence is not a mood. It is a settled refusal of the mercy God offers in the day of visitation.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines IMPEN'ITENCE as want of penitence or repentance; absence of contrition or sorrow for sin; obduracy; hardness of heart.
webster_full: IMPEN'ITENCE, IMPEN'ITENCY, noun — Want of penitence or repentance; absence of contrition or sorrow for sin; obduracy; hardness of heart. Final impenitence dooms the sinner to inevitable punishment.
He will advance from one degree of impenitence to another.
scriptures: Romans 2:5
But after thy hardness and impenitent heart treasurest up unto thyself wrath against the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God;
Proverbs 29:1
He, that being often reproved hardeneth his neck, shall suddenly be destroyed, and that without remedy.
corruption_summary: Modern counsel often renames impenitence as unreadiness, self-acceptance, or a wound that must not be called sin.
corruption_paragraphs: The old word required contrition. The new vocabulary prefers a man who is not yet ready, whose choices are a journey, or whose conscience should be soothed rather than struck. That is not mercy. It is a softer name for hardness of heart.

Scripture still gives space to repent, and still warns that the space can be despised. Impenitence treasures up wrath. The remedy is repentance toward God and faith in the Lord Jesus Christ, not a redescription of the sin.
roots_summary: Latin impenitentia is the want of repentance. The KJV uses the adjective impenitent of the heart that will not turn. No Strong's number is invented for the English noun.
roots_lines: Latin in + poeniteo — not repenting; absence of sorrow for sin.
KJV impenitent heart stands beside hardness and wrath (Rom 2:5).
No invented Strong's tag for the abstract English noun.
usage: Impenitence is want of repentance, not a neutral delay.
An often-reproved neck that hardens is near sudden ruin.
Use the space God gives to repent; do not rename hardness as health.

etymology: From Latin circumspicere, to look around: caution that attends to the facts of a case and the likely end of a course. Webster 1828 defines it as attention aimed at a correct course, or at avoiding danger.
biblical_def: Circumspection is watchful obedience, not nervous self-trust. The LORD commanded Israel, in all things He had said, to be circumspect, and to make no mention of the name of other gods (Exo 23:13). Paul charges the church to walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise (Eph 5:15). A prudent man foresees the evil and hides himself; the simple pass on and are punished (Prov 22:3). The virtue looks around because God has spoken, and because sin has consequences.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines CIRCUMSPECTION as caution; attention to all the facts and circumstances of a case, and to the natural or probable consequences of a measure, with a view to a correct course of conduct, or to avoid danger.
webster_full: CIRCUMSPECTION, noun — Caution; attention to all the facts and circumstances of a case, and to the natural or probable consequences of a measure, with a view to a correct course of conduct, or to avoid danger.
scriptures: Exodus 23:13
And in all things that I have said unto you be circumspect: and make no mention of the name of other gods, neither let it be heard out of thy mouth.
Ephesians 5:15
See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise,
corruption_summary: The age mocks circumspection as timidity or legalism, and praises impulse as courage.
corruption_paragraphs: Caution that asks what God has said, and what a course will cost, is now often called fear or smallness. Scripture calls it wisdom. The fool does not look around. He mentions other gods, walks as a fool, and is punished because he would not foresee the evil.

The opposite error makes circumspection a substitute for faith, a life of hedging that never obeys. Biblical circumspection is attention in order to do what the LORD has said, not delay dressed up as prudence.
roots_summary: Latin circum and specere mean to look around. The KJV uses circumspect and circumspectly for careful obedience. No Strong's number is invented for the English noun.
roots_lines: Latin circumspicere — to look around before acting.
KJV be circumspect is tied to refusing the names of other gods (Exo 23:13).
KJV walk circumspectly is set against walking as fools (Eph 5:15).
usage: Circumspection looks around in order to obey, not in order to stall.
Be circumspect in what God has said; do not name other gods.
Walk circumspectly, as the wise, not as fools.

etymology: From Latin assiduitas, constant presence, from sitting close to a work. Webster 1828 gives two senses: close application to a business, and attentive service rendered with zeal and constancy.
biblical_def: Assiduity is constant application, not a burst of zeal that dies. Keep the heart with all diligence, for out of it are the issues of life (Prov 4:23). Add to faith virtue, and to virtue knowledge, giving all diligence (2 Pet 1:5). Whatsoever you do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men (Col 3:23). The Christian virtue is not busyness for its own sake. It is steady labor under the eye of God, without sloth and without vainglory.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ASSIDU'ITY as constant or close application to any business or enterprise; diligence; and, in the plural, services rendered with zeal and constancy.
webster_full: ASSIDU'ITY, noun — Constant or close application to any business or enterprise; diligence.
Attention; attentiveness to persons. Assiduities, in the plural, are services rendered with zeal and constancy.
scriptures: Proverbs 4:23
Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life.
Colossians 3:23
And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men;
corruption_summary: Hustle makes assiduity a brand, and sloth calls steady work oppression; both miss labor unto the Lord.
corruption_paragraphs: One corruption turns constant application into a performance of grind, measured by applause and exhaustion. Another calls all steadiness legalism and leaves the hand idle. Scripture rejects both. Diligence belongs to the heart first, and the work is done as to the Lord, not unto men.
Assiduity in the second Webster sense, attentive service to persons, is likewise not flattery. It is constancy in a charge. The church needs that more than it needs another speech about balance.
roots_summary: Latin assiduitas is close, continued application. The KJV speaks of diligence and of doing the work heartily. No Strong's number is invented for the English noun.
roots_lines: Latin assiduus — sitting close to the work; constant.
KJV diligence guards the heart, from which life issues (Prov 4:23).
No invented Strong's tag for the later English noun assiduity.
usage: Assiduity is close application over time, not a single energetic day.
Do the work heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men.
Keep the heart with diligence before you boast of the schedule.

etymology: From Latin alacritas, from alacer, lively. Webster 1828 prefers the moral sense: cheerful readiness or promptitude to do some act; cheerful willingness.
biblical_def: Alacrity is cheerful readiness to obey, not a manufactured mood. Serve the LORD with gladness, and come before His presence with singing (Ps 100:2). God loves a cheerful giver, not a gift squeezed out by grudging or necessity (2 Cor 9:7). The psalmist made haste and delayed not to keep the commandments (Ps 119:60). Cheerful willingness is a fruit of a heart enlarged by God. It is not the same as noise, and it is not optional ornament on obedience.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ALAC'RITY as cheerfulness; more usually, a cheerful readiness or promptitude to do some act; cheerful willingness.
webster_full: ALAC'RITY, noun — Cheerfulness; gaiety; sprightliness; more usually, a cheerful readiness or promptitude to do some act; cheerful willingness; as, the soldiers advanced with alacrity to meet the enemy.
scriptures: Psalm 100:2
Serve the LORD with gladness: come before his presence with singing.
2 Corinthians 9:7
Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.
corruption_summary: Alacrity is flattened into personality or hype, while grudging obedience is treated as the serious kind.
corruption_paragraphs: Platforms sell cheer as a brand and call reluctance depth. Scripture does not. Gladness in the presence of the LORD, and cheerful giving, are commanded postures of the heart. A sour gift and a delayed commandment are not more spiritual for being heavy.
The other theft is counterfeit alacrity: volume without willingness, a smile laid over a heart that has not purposed the act. Webster's word is readiness to do the thing, not a display beside it.
roots_summary: Latin alacritas is liveliness of will. The KJV speaks of gladness, a cheerful giver, and haste to keep the commandment. No Strong's number is invented for the English noun.
roots_lines: Latin alacer — lively, cheerful, prompt.
KJV gladness and the cheerful giver carry the moral sense Webster names.
No invented Strong's tag for the English noun alacrity.
usage: Alacrity is cheerful willingness to do the act, not a mood for its own sake.
Serve the LORD with gladness; do not come before Him grudgingly.
Make haste to keep the commandment; delay is not depth.

etymology: From Latin carnalis, of the flesh. Webster 1828 defines carnality as fleshly lust and its indulgence, and as grossness of mind that loves sensual pleasures.
biblical_def: Carnality is the mind and life ordered by the flesh rather than by the Spirit. To be carnally minded is death; to be spiritually minded is life and peace (Rom 8:6). The carnal mind is enmity against God; it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be (Rom 8:7). Where there is envying, strife, and divisions, Paul says the church is yet carnal and walks as men (1 Cor 3:3). Carnality is not a private taste. It is hostility to God showing up in appetite and in the congregation.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines CARNALITY as fleshly lust, or desires, or the indulgence of those lusts; sensuality; and grossness of mind or desire; love of sensual pleasures.
webster_full: CARNALITY, noun — Fleshly lust, or desires, or the indulgence of those lusts; sensuality.
Grossness of mind or desire; love of sensual pleasures.
scriptures: Romans 8:6
For to be carnally minded is death; but to be spiritually minded is life and peace.
Romans 8:7
Because the carnal mind is enmity against God: for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be.
corruption_summary: The age renames carnality as authenticity, embodiment, or a healthy appetite, and treats enmity against God as self-expression.
corruption_paragraphs: Desire is now often its own credential. If the flesh wants it, the want is called honest. Paul does not speak that way. The carnal mind is death and enmity. It cannot be talked into subjection. It must be put off by union with Christ and walk in the Spirit.

A churchly form of the same corruption calls envy and party carnality a difference of style. Paul called that walking as men. Carnality in the pew is still carnality when it wears a religious argument.
roots_summary: Latin caro, flesh, gives the English family carnal and carnality. The KJV sets the carnal mind against the spiritual mind. No Strong's number is invented for the abstract noun.
roots_lines: Latin carnalis — pertaining to the flesh.
KJV carnally minded is death; the carnal mind is enmity against God (Rom 8:6-7).
No invented Strong's tag for the English noun carnality.
usage: Carnality is the flesh in charge of mind and life, not a neutral preference.
The carnal mind is enmity against God and is not subject to His law.
Envying and strife in the church are carnal, even when they quote a cause.

etymology: From Latin sensualitas, devotion to the senses. Webster 1828 defines sensuality as devotedness to the gratification of the bodily appetites, and free indulgence in carnal or sensual pleasures.
biblical_def: Sensuality is a life governed by bodily appetite rather than by the Spirit of God. James says the wisdom that does not descend from above is earthly, sensual, devilish (Jas 3:15). Jude names men who separate themselves, sensual, having not the Spirit (Jude 1:19). She that lives in pleasure is dead while she lives (1 Tim 5:6). The word is not a slur for having a body. It is the indictment of a mind that serves the senses and calls that wisdom.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SENSUAL'ITY as devotedness to the gratification of the bodily appetites; free indulgence in carnal or sensual pleasures.
webster_full: SENSUAL'ITY, noun — Devotedness to the gratification of the bodily appetites; free indulgence in carnal or sensual pleasures.
Those pamper'd animals that rage in savage sensuality.
They avoid dress, lest they should have affections tainted by any sensuality.
scriptures: James 3:15
This wisdom descendeth not from above, but is earthly, sensual, devilish.
Jude 1:19
These be they who separate themselves, sensual, having not the Spirit.
corruption_summary: Sensuality is marketed as liberation of the body, and abstinence is treated as the suspect thing.
corruption_paragraphs: The senses are God's gift. Devotedness to their gratification is not. James puts sensual wisdom in a triad with earthly and devilish. Jude puts the sensual man among those who have not the Spirit. That is a doctrinal claim, not a manners complaint.

A softer corruption keeps the indulgence and changes the noun: wellness, embodiment, being in touch with the body. If the life is still free indulgence of appetite, Webster's noun still fits, and so does the apostle's.
roots_summary: Latin sensus lies behind the English word. The KJV uses sensual for wisdom from below and for men without the Spirit. No Strong's number is invented for the abstract noun.
roots_lines: Latin sensualis — pertaining to the gratification of sense.
KJV sensual describes wisdom not from above (Jas 3:15) and men having not the Spirit (Jude 1:19).
No invented Strong's tag for the English noun sensuality.
usage: Sensuality is devotedness to bodily appetite, not the mere fact of having a body.
Wisdom that is earthly and sensual is also devilish.
The sensual separator is marked by not having the Spirit.

etymology: From Latin voluptuosus, full of pleasure, from voluptas. Webster 1828 defines voluptuousness as luxuriousness and addictedness to pleasure or sensual gratification.
biblical_def: Voluptuousness is addictedness to luxury and sensual pleasure. James rebukes those who have lived in pleasure on the earth and been wanton, nourishing their hearts as in a day of slaughter (Jas 5:5). The rich man was clothed in purple and fine linen and fared sumptuously every day, and the account does not treat that ease as innocence (Luke 16:19). In the last days men are lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God (2 Tim 3:4). Soft living can choke the word as surely as open vice.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines VOLUP'TUOUSNESS as luxuriousness; addictedness to pleasure or sensual gratification.
webster_full: VOLUP'TUOUSNESS, noun — Luxuriousness; addictedness to pleasure or sensual gratification.
Where no voluptuousness yet all delight.
scriptures: James 5:5
Ye have lived in pleasure on the earth, and been wanton; ye have nourished your hearts, as in a day of slaughter.
Luke 16:19
There was a certain rich man, which was clothed in purple and fine linen, and fared sumptuously every day:
corruption_summary: Luxury is rebranded as self-care or success, and addictedness to pleasure is no longer named as a vice.
corruption_paragraphs: The old noun was an accusation. The new market makes the same life a goal: sumptuous fare, soft days, pleasure as the measure of a life well lived. James calls that nourishing the heart for slaughter. Paul lists lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God among the marks of perilous times.

Delight itself is not the sin. Webster's own illustration can say there is delight where there is no voluptuousness. The corruption is addictedness: pleasure as lord. The cure is not scorn of every good gift, but a heart that loves God more than the gift.
roots_summary: Latin voluptas is pleasure. The KJV speaks of living in pleasure, faring sumptuously, and loving pleasures more than God. No Strong's number is invented for the English noun.
roots_lines: Latin voluptas — pleasure; voluptuousness is addictedness to it.
KJV lived in pleasure and fared sumptuously name the life Webster defines.
No invented Strong's tag for the English noun.
usage: Voluptuousness is addictedness to luxury and sensual pleasure, not every lawful delight.
Living in pleasure and faring sumptuously every day is not a neutral lifestyle.
Lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God are in peril, not in bloom.
